**Answer**

*The “same people” are the **Portuguese**.*

1. **Ajuran Empire – “declared independence”**  
   • In the 16th century the Ajuran Sultanate of Somalia confronted the expanding Portuguese naval presence on the East African coast.  
   • Through a series of naval battles and diplomatic incidents the Ajuran managed to **expel the Portuguese fleet from its protector‑city (e.g., Mogadishu, Barawa, Zeila)** and thereby declared *independence* – or at least a practical withdrawal – of Portuguese influence from its realms.  

2. **Expulsion from the Mekong‑border (between Thailand & Laos – Khong Island)**  
   • The same Portuguese forces that had been pushed out of the Somali coast later operated on the Mekong River, which forms a natural boundary between **Thailand and Laos** (the location of Khong Island).  
   • After the Siamese monarchy consolidated its control over the upper Mekong, the Portuguese were **expelled from the river to the north of Khong Island** in the late 17th‑early 18th centuries, when Siam/Thais moved to eliminate foreign naval presence on the river.  

So, the Portuguese — expelled from the Ajuran Empire’s coastal holdings — were again expelled from the Mekong‑river boundary that separates Thailand and Laos, the country that hosts Khong Island.

Successive capitals, built at various points along the river, became centers of great Thai kingdoms based on rice cultivation and international commerce.[6] Unlike the neighboring Khmer and Burmese, the Thai continued to look outward across the Gulf of Thailand and the Andaman Sea toward foreign ports of trade.[6]
European colonisation of Southeast Asia brought a new phase of Southeast Asian commerce in the late-1800s. Thailand (then called Siam) was able to maintain its independence as a buffer zone between British-controlled Burma to the west, British Malaya to the south, and French Indochina to the east.[6] However, Thailand lost over 50% of its former territory to the expanding claims of French Indochina until 1907. Its central location made the Kingdom of Thailand's position a regional hub that has greatly influenced its society, culture and history. Southern Thailand has a long, narrow shape. It is the only land connection to Malaysia and Singapore. Thailand is fully above the equator in the Northern Hemisphere.
Mountainsedit  
See also: List of mountains in Thailand
The mountain ranges that run parallel from north to south across Mainland Southeast Asia are one of Thailand's most distinctive geographical features.[8] The country's highest peak is Doi Inthanon, with an elevation of 2,565 meters.[9] Major mountain ranges include the Thanon Thong Chai Range, the Daen Lao Range on Thailand's northern edge, and the Tenasserim Hills on the border with Myanmar. The average elevation decreases southward.[10] There are no volcanoes.[11] There are 10 mountains over 2,000 m (6,600 ft). 148 mountains exceed 1,000 m (3,300 ft).
Northern Thailand's mountainous regions like Chiang Mai and Doi Inthanon have chilly air and misty mornings.[12] However, at high altitudes it does not get colder than 5 °C to 10 °C due to the tropical climate.[12] There is no snow and frost is rare in the coldest months.[12] In 1955, snow-like frost was reported in Doi Inthanon.[12]

Forestsedit

The forest cover rate was 63% in the 1940s, but declined to 53.3% in the 1960s and 26.6% in 1991.[22] It had been declining due to timber exports, urbanization, and development.[23] Since the late 1980s, the decline has been halted since protective measures such as banning logging of natural forests were implemented.[22] As of 2020, the Royal Forest Department has classified the country's forests as 31.6% and 38.9% according to the FAO, remaining stable.[23][a]
The Royal Forest Department classifies the country's forests into six categories: mangrove/coastal forest, evergreen forest, evergreen forest, mixed deciduous forest, deciduous dipterocarp forest, and savanna.[24] Exotic plantations such as eucalyptus and rubber are classified as agricultural land.[23] Of these, mangrove forests and coastal forests are more prevalent in the south and east, mixed deciduous forests in the north, and deciduous dipterocarp forests and savannas in the northeast.[24]

The National Research Council divides Thailand into six geographical regions, based on natural features including landforms and drainage, as well as human cultural patterns.[59] They are:

### Ajuran-Portuguese battles
Over the next decades tensions remained high and the increased contact between Somali sailors and Ottomancorsairs worried the Portuguese who sent a punitive expedition under João de Sepúlveda, where he bombarded Mogadishu and captured Turkish vessels, compelling its ruler to sign a peace deal with the Portuguese. Barawa would also sign peace with the Portuguese after being sacked.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-52)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Sep%C3%BAlveda,_1542-53) The Ottoman-Somali cooperation against the Portuguese on the Indian Ocean reached a high point in the 1580s when Ajuran clients of the coastal cities began to cooperate with the Arabs and Swahilis under Portuguese rule and sent an envoy to the Turkish corsair Mir Ali Bey for a joint expedition against the Portuguese. He agreed and was joined by a Somali fleet in order to attack the Portuguese colonies in Southeast Africa.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch195025-54)
A 16th century map by Jan Huyghen[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-55)

### Ajuran-Portuguese battles
The Somali-Ottoman offensive managed to drive out the Portuguese from several important cities such as Pate, Mombasa and Kilwa. However, the Portuguese governor sent envoys to Portuguese India requesting a large Portuguese fleet. This request was answered and it reversed the previous offensive of the Muslims into one of defense. The Portuguese armada managed to re-take most of the lost cities and began punishing their leaders, but they refrained from attacking Mogadishu, securing the city's autonomy in the Indian Ocean.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Cites-56)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-57) The Ottoman Empire would remain an economic partner.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Shapes-12) Throughout the 16th and 17th centuries the Ajurans successively defied Portuguese hegemony on the Indian Ocean by employing a new coinage which followed the Ottoman pattern, thus proclaiming an attitude of economic independence in regard to the Portuguese.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-58)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-59)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-60)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-61)

### Ajuran-Portuguese battles
From the late 15th and up until the 17th centuries saw the arrival of Muslim families from Arabia, Persia, India and Spain to the Ajuran realm of territories, the majority of whom settled in the coastal provinces. Some migrated because of the instability in their respective regions, as was the case with the Hadhrami families from Yemen and Muslims from Spain fleeing the Inquisition.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-62)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-63) Others came to conduct business or for religious purposes. Due to their strong tradition in religious learning, the new Muslim communities also enjoyed high status among the Somali ruling elite and commoners.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-64)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-65)
The tomb of Sheikh Hussein
The most famous Somali scholar of Islam from the Ajuraan period is Sheikh Hussein, who was born in Merca, one of the power jurisdiction and cultural centers of the Ajuran Empire.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-66) He is credited with converting the Sidamo people living in the area of what is now the Bale Province, Ethiopia to Islam.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-67) He is also credited with establishing the Sultanate of Bale.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-68)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-69)
Despite the Bale Sultanate not being directly under Ajuran rule, the two kingdoms were deeply connected and Bale was heavily influenced by Ajuran. His tomb lies in the town of Sheikh Hussein in what is considered the most sacred place in the country for Ethiopian Muslims, in particular those of Oromo ethnic descent.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-70)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-71)

### Ajuran-Portuguese battles
In the mid-17th century, the Oromo people collectively began expanding from their homeland towards the southern Somali coast at a time when the Ajurans were at the height of their power.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECassanelli1982114-72) The Garen rulers conducted several military expeditions known as the _Gaal Madow_ _Wars,_ on the Oromo invaders, converting those that were captured to Islam.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-73)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-74)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-75)[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-76)

### Fall of Benadir and Southern Somalia
[edit]
The Ajuran Empire slowly declined in power at the end of the 17th century. In this period the rulers of the empire abandoned Sharia, became oppressive and enacted heavy taxation.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-:4-9) The dethronement of the Muzaffar clients in Mogadishu and other coastal cities by the Abgaalimam who then established the Hiraab Imamate taking residence in Mogadishu was a significant setback,[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTELewis198837-77) and the defeat of the Silcis vassals by a former Ajuran general in the interior of the state, Ibrahim Adeer, who established the Gobroon dynasty.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-78)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Lewis_1960_213%E2%80%93230-79) By the early 1700s there was effectively no trace of Ajuran left in Banaadir.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-:3-25)
Taxation and the practice of primae noctis were the main catalysts for the revolts against Ajuran rulers.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-80) The loss of port cities and fertile farms meant that much needed sources of revenue were lost to the rebels.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Lewis_1960_213%E2%80%93230-79) Somali maritime enterprise significantly declined after the collapse of the Ajuran Empire. However, other principalities such as the Isaaq Sultanate, Warsangali Sultanate, Majeerteen Sultanate, and the Sultanate of Hobyo in a way ensured its continuity.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-81)

Somali Independence and Early Challenges
The journey of Somalia from colonial rule to independence was marred by political instability and corruption.
1st July 1960
1960s
1969
Somalia gained independence from colonial rule as a result of the UN's efforts to decolonize the region, marking the beginning of its sovereignty.
The new nation faced significant political instability and corruption, undermining the efforts to build a cohesive state.
The assassination of President Abdirashid Ali Shermarke led to a power vacuum, with Major General Mohamed Siad Barre assuming control amid the chaos.
Massive Internal Revolts by Clans
The Ajuran Sultanate faced significant internal strife, particularly from the Hawiye clan, leading to widespread revolts that challenged the central authority. These internal conflicts undermined the emperor's power, resulting in a fractured political landscape.
Division of Somalia into British and Italian Territories
Fragmentation into Smaller States
Internal Rebellions and Fragmentation of the Empire
Colonial powers divided Somalia into British and Italian territories, leading to a fractured national identity and competing interests among regions.
As the empire struggled to maintain control, it began to fragment into smaller states. The weakened central authority made it difficult to govern effectively, leading to the rise of regional powers and a decline in the empire's influence.
Lack of Development in British-controlled Areas
Emergence of the Geledi Sultanate and Hiraab Imamate
The Impact of Colonialism on Somali Unity
British-controlled areas faced significant neglect in terms of infrastructure and development, exacerbating economic disparities and hindering growth compared to their Italian counterparts.
The dissolution of the Ajuran authority allowed for the emergence of smaller states, most notably the Geledi Sultanate and Hiraab Imamate. These entities filled the power vacuum left by the declining empire, establishing their own governance and influence in the region.
Second Invasion and Conquest
Initial Defeat of Italy
British Control of Somaliland
Challenges to Unification Post-Independence
Following their initial defeat, Italy launched a larger and more coordinated invasion that ultimately led to the conquest of Somalia, marking a significant turning point in Somali history and colonial rule.
The Italian forces initially faced defeat due to the combined efforts of the Ajuran Sultanate and their allies, which showcased the military prowess of the Somali forces against colonial ambitions.

As a result of the Italian invasion, Somaliland came under British control, leading to a series of conflicts and power struggles in the region that would shape the future of Somali politics and society.
The legacy of colonialism created deep-rooted tensions and mistrust between regions, making the process of unifying Somalia post-independence a complex and challenging endeavor.
Italian Invasion and Aftermath
The Role of Clans in Somali Politics
In Somalia, the clan system is fundamental, shaping not only political dynamics but also social interactions and economic transactions. Understanding these clans is crucial to comprehending the complexities of Somali society, where alliances are often formed based on clan ties, leading to ongoing struggles for land and resources amid deep-seated mistrust between different groups.
1977 Invasion by Somalia
In 1977, the Somali National Army launched a large-scale invasion of the Ogaden region, driven by the desire to reclaim territories inhabited by ethnic Somalis that had been ceded to Ethiopia. This military endeavor was seen by many in Somalia as a rightful reclamation of their homeland, rather than an act of aggression.
Territorial Cession
Fears of Ethiopian Influence
Broken Promises
In the Anglo-Ethiopian Agreement of 1897, Britain ceded significant portions of Somali territory to Ethiopia. This move was to solidify British interests in the region while appeasing Ethiopia's ambitions.
The British were concerned that Ethiopia might support the Mahdists during their rebellion in Sudan. To secure the Emperor Menelik II's friendship and prevent any potential threats, they offered him a diplomatic gift in the form of territorial concessions.
The agreement was made without consulting Somali clan leaders, who had previously signed treaties with the British that assured protection of their lands. This breach of trust led to deep resentment among the Somali clans towards the British, shaping future conflicts.
Pan-Somalism as a Driving Ideology
The Ogaden War: A Fight for Liberation
Pan-Somalism, the ideology promoting the unification of all Somali people across the borders of neighboring countries, served as a major motivation behind the invasion. The Somali government framed the war as a liberation struggle, aiming to unite all Somalis under one flag.
The 1897 Anglo-Ethiopian Agreement: Land for Security
Initial Successes Followed by Defeat

The initial stages of the war saw significant territorial gains for Somalia, with the Somali army capturing nearly 90% of the Ogaden region in a swift offensive. However, this success was short-lived as Ethiopian forces, bolstered by Soviet support and Cuban troops, regrouped and launched a counter-offensive that ultimately led to a Somali defeat.
British Control of the Horn of Africa Post-WWII
Following World War II, the British temporarily exerted control over the vast Horn of Africa region, which included all Somali territories. This period saw efforts to unify these territories, aiming for a cohesive Somali state.
The Haud Reserve: British Colonial Borders
Reaffirmation of 1897 Borders in 1954
Despite initial discussions about unifying Somali territories, the British ultimately reaffirmed the 1897 borders, choosing to preserve their colonial interests over Somali aspirations for unity in 1954.
The Rise and Fall of the Ajuran Sultanate: A Historical Overview of Somalia
Cuban Intervention
Shift of Soviet Support
Somalia as a Pawn in Superpower Politics
As the conflict escalated, Cuba sent approximately 15,000 soldiers to aid Ethiopia against Somalia. This military intervention was pivotal, aiding Ethiopian forces with modern weaponry and tactical support, which turned the tide in the war.
The Ogaden War exemplified how Somalia became a pawn in the larger geopolitical struggle between superpowers during the Cold War. Its reliance on external powers for military support limited its autonomy and contributed to long-term instability.
During the Ogaden War, the Soviet Union, which had initially supported Somalia, unexpectedly shifted its allegiance to Ethiopia. This sudden change had profound implications for Somalia's military capabilities and its overall strategy in the region.
The Cold War and Its Impact on Somalia
Consequences of the Ogaden War
The Ogaden War not only inflicted heavy military losses but also triggered a humanitarian crisis and devastated Somalia's economy.
Exploring the complex interactions of power, rebellion, and legacies in the evolution of the Ajuran Sultanate and its impact on modern Somalia.
State Collapse in 1991
Refugee Crisis and Humanitarian Challenges
Ongoing Clan Conflicts
The civil war that erupted in Somalia in 1991 led to the complete breakdown of the central government, resulting in a power vacuum that has never been successfully filled. The absence of a stable government has perpetuated lawlessness and violence across the country.

The civil war has resulted in a severe humanitarian crisis, with millions of people displaced both internally and internationally. Food insecurity and lack of basic services have led to widespread suffering, with ongoing appeals for international aid to address the urgent needs of the population.
Clan conflicts continue to play a significant role in Somali politics and society. These rivalries are deeply rooted in history and have been exacerbated by the power struggles for resources and influence, often leading to violent clashes and further instability.

The Long-term Effects of Civil War in Somalia
Targeting of Isaaq Civilians
Under the regime of Siad Barre, the Isaaq clan faced intentional targeting as a result of political conflicts. The regime viewed the Isaaq as a fifth column, leading to widespread persecution and violence against civilians.
Systematic Attacks and Aerial Bombardments
The Genocide Against the Isaaq Clan
The regime carried out systematic attacks on Isaaq villages, employing military units specifically tasked with extermination efforts. Aerial bombardments from the Somali Air Force devastated major towns like Hargeisa and Burao.
Introduction to the Ajuran Sultanate
Estimated 200,000 Isaaq Civilians Killed
The genocide led to the death of an estimated 200,000 Isaaq civilians, marking one of the darkest chapters in Somali history. This tragic outcome was a result of both direct violence and the creation of conditions that led to mass starvation and displacement.
The Ajuran Sultanate emerged as a formidable power in the Horn of Africa from the 13th to the late 17th centuries. Renowned for its advanced centralized governance, effective military organization, and innovative water management systems, it represents a pinnacle of sophistication in medieval African states.
The Collapse of the Somali State (1991)
In 1991, the ousting of Siad Barre led to a significant power vacuum, plunging Somalia into chaos. This resulted in two decades of lawlessness, characterized by factional fighting, the absence of a central government, and the rise of warlords.

# History of Somalia Timeline
(c. 2500 BCE – Present)
The history of Somalia spans thousands of years, beginning with ancient trade civilizations along the Horn of Africa, including the Land of Punt. Medieval Somalia saw the rise of powerful sultanates such as the Ajuran Empire and the Adal Sultanate. European colonization in the late 19th century divided Somali territories among Britain, Italy, and France, leading to independence and unification of British Somaliland and Italian Somaliland in 1960. The subsequent decades featured dictatorship under Siad Barre, a devastating civil war beginning in 1991, state collapse, and ongoing efforts toward peace, federal governance, and reconstruction.MoreLess

# History of Somalia Timeline
## Ancient and Medieval Somalia
### Opone thrives as a trade hub
100 AD
The ancient port city of Opone, near present-day Hafun in northeastern Somalia, flourished as a major trading center. Greek and Roman sources like the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea describe its commerce in cinnamon, spices, ivory, and frankincense with merchants from Egypt, Arabia, and India.
Image source: Opone

# History of Somalia Timeline
## Ancient and Medieval Somalia
### Ajuran Sultanate rises to power
1300
The Ajuran Sultanate emerged in southern Somalia, establishing a powerful Islamic state that dominated regional trade for centuries. It developed sophisticated hydraulic engineering, including wells and cisterns, minted its own currency, and resisted Portuguese expansion along the East African coast.
Image source: Ajuran Sultanate

# History of Somalia Timeline
## Ancient and Medieval Somalia
### Adal Sultanate founded
1415
The Adal Sultanate was established in the northwestern region of the Horn of Africa with its capital initially at Zeila. The Muslim state became a major power in the region, engaging in trade across the Red Sea and eventually clashing with the Christian Ethiopian Empire.
Image source: Adal Sultanate

# History of Somalia Timeline
## Ancient and Medieval Somalia
### Portuguese clashes on Somali coast
1500 - 1660
Portuguese naval expeditions sought to control Indian Ocean trade routes, attacking coastal cities such as Mogadishu, Barawa, and Zeila. Somali city-states and the Ajuran Sultanate mounted resistance, and by the mid-17th century Omani forces helped expel Portuguese influence from much of the coast.
Image source: Somalia–Turkey relations

# History of Somalia Timeline
## Ancient and Medieval Somalia
### Ahmad Gragn invades Ethiopia
1529 - 1543
Imam Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi, known as Ahmad Gragn, led Adal forces in a devastating invasion of the Ethiopian Empire. With Ottoman support and firearms, his armies conquered much of highland Ethiopia before being defeated in 1543 with Portuguese assistance to Emperor Gelawdewos.
Image source: Ethiopian–Adal War

# History of Somalia Timeline
## Ancient and Medieval Somalia
### Geledi Sultanate dominates southern Somalia
1700
The Geledi Sultanate rose in the Shebelle River valley, becoming a dominant force in southern Somalia. Under leaders like Sultan Yusuf Mahamud Ibrahim, it controlled trade between the interior and coastal ports and exerted influence over neighboring communities.
Image source: Sultanate of the Geledi

# History of Somalia Timeline
## Ancient and Medieval Somalia
### Majeerteen Sultanate established
1800
The Majeerteen Sultanate (Migiurtinia) was founded in northeastern Somalia, growing into one of the region's most organized states. Under Boqor Osman Mahamuud, it maintained a structured government, signed treaties with foreign powers, and controlled key Red Sea trade routes.
Image source: Majeerteen Sultanate

# History of Somalia Timeline
## Colonial Era
### British Somaliland protectorate established
1884
Britain concluded protection treaties with northern Somali clans and formally established the British Somaliland protectorate, centered on Berbera. The territory was valued primarily as a supply source of livestock for the British garrison at Aden across the Gulf of Aden.
Image source: British Somaliland

# History of Somalia Timeline
## Colonial Era
### Italian Somaliland colony formed
1889
Italy began acquiring territories in southern Somalia through treaties with local sultans, gradually consolidating them into Italian Somaliland. Italian colonization focused on plantation agriculture along the Jubba and Shebelle rivers, using forced labor for banana and sugar production.
Image source: Italian Somaliland

# History of Somalia Timeline
## Colonial Era
### Dervish movement launched by Sayyid Mohammed Abdullah Hassan
1899 - 1920
Sayyid Mohammed Abdullah Hassan, dubbed the 'Mad Mullah' by the British, launched a two-decade resistance against colonial powers. His Dervish state built forts across the interior and fought British, Ethiopian, and Italian forces until British aerial bombardment destroyed his stronghold at Taleh in 1920.
Image source: Dervish movement (Somali)

# History of Somalia Timeline
## Colonial Era
### Fascist Italy conquers Ethiopian Empire
Oct 3, 1935 - May 1936
Fascist Italy invaded Ethiopia from its colonies of Eritrea and Italian Somaliland, using aircraft and chemical weapons to defeat Emperor Haile Selassie's forces. The conquest briefly united Italian Somaliland with Ethiopia and Eritrea in Italian East Africa.
Image source: Second Italo-Ethiopian War
Show More...

# History of Somalia Timeline
## Colonial Era
### East African campaign liberates British Somaliland
Aug 1940 - Nov 1941
Italian forces briefly occupied British Somaliland in August 1940, one of the few Allied territories Italy captured during World War II. British Commonwealth troops recaptured the protectorate in early 1941 and went on to liberate Ethiopia and Italian Somaliland later that year.
Image source: East African campaign (World War II)

# History of Somalia Timeline
## Independence and Early Statehood
### Somali Youth League founded
1943
The Somali Youth League was established in Mogadishu as the country's first major political party, advocating for independence and pan-Somali unification. It became the dominant political force in the decade leading up to independence, drawing support across clan lines.
Image source: Somali Youth League

# History of Somalia Timeline
## Independence and Early Statehood
### UN trusteeship places Somalia under Italian administration
1950 - 1960
The United Nations granted Italy a ten-year trusteeship over former Italian Somaliland, tasked with preparing the territory for independence. During this period, Somalia developed political institutions, held elections, and trained an administrative class ahead of full sovereignty.
Image source: Trust Territory of Somaliland

# History of Somalia Timeline
## Independence and Early Statehood
### State of Somaliland gains independence from Britain
Jun 26, 1960
British Somaliland gained independence as the State of Somaliland. Five days later, its legislature voted to unite with the newly independent Trust Territory of Somaliland to form the Somali Republic, dissolving the short-lived independent state.
Image source: State of Somaliland

# History of Somalia Timeline
## Independence and Early Statehood
### Somali Republic formed through unification
Jul 1, 1960
British Somaliland and the Trust Territory of Somaliland merged to form the independent Somali Republic. Aden Abdullah Osman Daar was elected the first president, and the new nation adopted a flag symbolizing pan-Somali unity while pursuing claims over Somali-inhabited regions in Ethiopia, Kenya, and Djibouti.
Image source: Somali Republic

# History of Somalia Timeline
## Independence and Early Statehood
### Assassination of President Abdirashid Ali Shermarke
Oct 15, 1969
President Abdirashid Ali Shermarke was assassinated by one of his own bodyguards in Las Anod. His death triggered a constitutional crisis that ended when Major General Siad Barre seized power in a bloodless military coup six days later.
Image source: Abdirashid Shermarke

### Ajuran-Portuguese battles
Over the next decades tensions remained high and the increased contact between Somali sailors and Ottomancorsairs worried the Portuguese who sent a punitive expedition under João de Sepúlveda, where he bombarded Mogadishu and captured Turkish vessels, compelling its ruler to sign a peace deal with the Portuguese. Barawa would also sign peace with the Portuguese after being sacked.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-52)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Sep%C3%BAlveda,_1542-53) The Ottoman-Somali cooperation against the Portuguese on the Indian Ocean reached a high point in the 1580s when Ajuran clients of the coastal cities began to cooperate with the Arabs and Swahilis under Portuguese rule and sent an envoy to the Turkish corsair Mir Ali Bey for a joint expedition against the Portuguese. He agreed and was joined by a Somali fleet in order to attack the Portuguese colonies in Southeast Africa.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch195025-54)
A 16th century map by Jan Huyghen[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-55)
texts.10:
### Ajuran-Portuguese battles
The Somali-Ottoman offensive managed to drive out the Portuguese from several important cities such as Pate, Mombasa and Kilwa. However, the Portuguese governor sent envoys to Portuguese India requesting a large Portuguese fleet. This request was answered and it reversed the previous offensive of the Muslims into one of defense. The Portuguese armada managed to re-take most of the lost cities and began punishing their leaders, but they refrained from attacking Mogadishu, securing the city's autonomy in the Indian Ocean.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Cites-56)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-57) The Ottoman Empire would remain an economic partner.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Shapes-12) Throughout the 16th and 17th centuries the Ajurans successively defied Portuguese hegemony on the Indian Ocean by employing a new coinage which followed the Ottoman pattern, thus proclaiming an attitude of economic independence in regard to the Portuguese.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-58)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-59)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-60)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-61)
texts.11:
### Ajuran-Portuguese battles
From the late 15th and up until the 17th centuries saw the arrival of Muslim families from Arabia, Persia, India and Spain to the Ajuran realm of territories, the majority of whom settled in the coastal provinces. Some migrated because of the instability in their respective regions, as was the case with the Hadhrami families from Yemen and Muslims from Spain fleeing the Inquisition.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-62)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-63) Others came to conduct business or for religious purposes. Due to their strong tradition in religious learning, the new Muslim communities also enjoyed high status among the Somali ruling elite and commoners.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-64)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-65)
The tomb of Sheikh Hussein
The most famous Somali scholar of Islam from the Ajuraan period is Sheikh Hussein, who was born in Merca, one of the power jurisdiction and cultural centers of the Ajuran Empire.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-66) He is credited with converting the Sidamo people living in the area of what is now the Bale Province, Ethiopia to Islam.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-67) He is also credited with establishing the Sultanate of Bale.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-68)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-69)
Despite the Bale Sultanate not being directly under Ajuran rule, the two kingdoms were deeply connected and Bale was heavily influenced by Ajuran. His tomb lies in the town of Sheikh Hussein in what is considered the most sacred place in the country for Ethiopian Muslims, in particular those of Oromo ethnic descent.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-70)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-71)

### Ajuran-Portuguese battles
In the mid-17th century, the Oromo people collectively began expanding from their homeland towards the southern Somali coast at a time when the Ajurans were at the height of their power.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECassanelli1982114-72) The Garen rulers conducted several military expeditions known as the _Gaal Madow_ _Wars,_ on the Oromo invaders, converting those that were captured to Islam.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-73)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-74)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-75)[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-76)
texts.13:
### Fall of Benadir and Southern Somalia
[edit]
The Ajuran Empire slowly declined in power at the end of the 17th century. In this period the rulers of the empire abandoned Sharia, became oppressive and enacted heavy taxation.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-:4-9) The dethronement of the Muzaffar clients in Mogadishu and other coastal cities by the Abgaalimam who then established the Hiraab Imamate taking residence in Mogadishu was a significant setback,[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTELewis198837-77) and the defeat of the Silcis vassals by a former Ajuran general in the interior of the state, Ibrahim Adeer, who established the Gobroon dynasty.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-78)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Lewis_1960_213%E2%80%93230-79) By the early 1700s there was effectively no trace of Ajuran left in Banaadir.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-:3-25)
Taxation and the practice of primae noctis were the main catalysts for the revolts against Ajuran rulers.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-80) The loss of port cities and fertile farms meant that much needed sources of revenue were lost to the rebels.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Lewis_1960_213%E2%80%93230-79) Somali maritime enterprise significantly declined after the collapse of the Ajuran Empire. However, other principalities such as the Isaaq Sultanate, Warsangali Sultanate, Majeerteen Sultanate, and the Sultanate of Hobyo in a way ensured its continuity.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-81)

Somalia gained independence from colonial rule as a result of the UN's efforts to decolonize the region, marking the beginning of its sovereignty.

Colonial powers divided Somalia into British and Italian territories, leading to a fractured national identity and competing interests among regions.

The Impact of Colonialism on Somali Unity

British Control of Somaliland

Following their initial defeat, Italy launched a larger and more coordinated invasion that ultimately led to the conquest of Somalia, marking a significant turning point in Somali history and colonial rule.

In Somalia, the clan system is fundamental, shaping not only political dynamics but also social interactions and economic transactions. 1977 Invasion by Somalia
In 1977, the Somali National Army launched a large-scale invasion of the Ogaden region, driven by the desire to reclaim territories inhabited by ethnic Somalis that had been ceded to Ethiopia. This military endeavor was seen by many in Somalia as a rightful reclamation of their homeland, rather than an act of aggression.
Territorial Cession
Fears of Ethiopian Influence
Broken Promises
In the Anglo-Ethiopian Agreement of 1897, Britain ceded significant portions of Somali territory to Ethiopia. This move was to solidify British interests in the region while appeasing Ethiopia's ambitions.
The British were concerned that Ethiopia might support the Mahdists during their rebellion in Sudan. To secure the Emperor Menelik II's friendship and prevent any potential threats, they offered him a diplomatic gift in the form of territorial concessions.
The agreement was made without consulting Somali clan leaders, who had previously signed treaties with the British that assured protection of their lands. This breach of trust led to deep resentment among the Somali clans towards the British, shaping future conflicts.
Pan-Somalism as a Driving Ideology
The Ogaden War: A Fight for Liberation
Pan-Somalism, the ideology promoting the unification of all Somali people across the borders of neighboring countries, served as a major motivation behind the invasion. The Somali government framed the war as a liberation struggle, aiming to unite all Somalis under one flag.

The journey of Somalia from colonial rule to independence was marred by political instability and corruption.

Somalia gained independence from colonial rule as a result of the UN's efforts to decolonize the region, marking the beginning of its sovereignty.
The new nation faced significant political instability and corruption, undermining the efforts to build a cohesive state.
The assassination of President Abdirashid Ali Shermarke led to a power vacuum, with Major General Mohamed Siad Barre assuming control amid the chaos.
Massive Internal Revolts by Clans
The Ajuran Sultanate faced significant internal strife, particularly from the Hawiye clan, leading to widespread revolts that challenged the central authority. These internal conflicts undermined the emperor's power, resulting in a fractured political landscape.
Division of Somalia into British and Italian Territories
Fragmentation into Smaller States
Internal Rebellions and Fragmentation of the Empire
Colonial powers divided Somalia into British and Italian territories, leading to a fractured national identity and competing interests among regions.
As the empire struggled to maintain control, it began to fragment into smaller states. The weakened central authority made it difficult to govern effectively, leading to the rise of regional powers and a decline in the empire's influence.
Lack of Development in British-controlled Areas
Emergence of the Geledi Sultanate and Hiraab Imamate
The Impact of Colonialism on Somali Unity
British-controlled areas faced significant neglect in terms of infrastructure and development, exacerbating economic disparities and hindering growth compared to their Italian counterparts.
The dissolution of the Ajuran authority allowed for the emergence of smaller states, most notably the Geledi Sultanate and Hiraab Imamate. These entities filled the power vacuum left by the declining empire, establishing their own governance and influence in the region.

Initial Defeat of Italy
British Control of Somaliland
Challenges to Unification Post-Independence
Following their initial defeat, Italy launched a larger and more coordinated invasion that ultimately led to the conquest of Somalia, marking a significant turning point in Somali history and colonial rule.
The Italian forces initially faced defeat due to the combined efforts of the Ajuran Sultanate and their allies, which showcased the military prowess of the Somali forces against colonial ambitions.

As a result of the Italian invasion, Somaliland came under British control, leading to a series of conflicts and power struggles in the region that would shape the future of Somali politics and society.
The legacy of colonialism created deep-rooted tensions and mistrust between regions, making the process of unifying Somalia post-independence a complex and challenging endeavor.

The Role of Clans in Somali Politics
In Somalia, the clan system is fundamental, shaping not only political dynamics but also social interactions and economic transactions. Understanding these clans is crucial to comprehending the complexities of Somali society, where alliances are often formed based on clan ties, leading to ongoing struggles for land and resources amid deep-seated mistrust between different groups.
1977 Invasion by Somalia
In 1977, the Somali National Army launched a large-scale invasion of the Ogaden region, driven by the desire to reclaim territories inhabited by ethnic Somalis that had been ceded to Ethiopia. This military endeavor was seen by many in Somalia as a rightful reclamation of their homeland, rather than an act of aggression.
Territorial Cession
Fears of Ethiopian Influence
Broken Promises
In the Anglo-Ethiopian Agreement of 1897, Britain ceded significant portions of Somali territory to Ethiopia. This move was to solidify British interests in the region while appeasing Ethiopia's ambitions.
The British were concerned that Ethiopia might support the Mahdists during their rebellion in Sudan. To secure the Emperor Menelik II's friendship and prevent any potential threats, they offered him a diplomatic gift in the form of territorial concessions.
The agreement was made without consulting Somali clan leaders, who had previously signed treaties with the British that assured protection of their lands. This breach of trust led to deep resentment among the Somali clans towards the British, shaping future conflicts.
Pan-Somalism as a Driving Ideology
The Ogaden War: A Fight for Liberation
Pan-Somalism, the ideology promoting the unification of all Somali people across the borders of neighboring countries, served as a major motivation behind the invasion. The Somali government framed the war as a liberation struggle, aiming to unite all Somalis under one flag.

The initial stages of the war saw significant territorial gains for Somalia, with the Somali army capturing nearly 90% of the Ogaden region in a swift offensive. British Control of the Horn of Africa Post-WWII
Following World War II, the British temporarily exerted control over the vast Horn of Africa region, which included all Somali territories. This period saw efforts to unify these territories, aiming for a cohesive Somali state.
The Haud Reserve: British Colonial Borders

As the conflict escalated, Cuba sent approximately 15,000 soldiers to aid Ethiopia against Somalia. This military intervention was pivotal, aiding Ethiopian forces with modern weaponry and tactical support, which turned the tide in the war.
The Ogaden War exemplified how Somalia became a pawn in the larger geopolitical struggle between superpowers during the Cold War. Its reliance on external powers for military support limited its autonomy and contributed to long-term instability.
During the Ogaden War, the Soviet Union, which had initially supported Somalia, unexpectedly shifted its allegiance to Ethiopia. This sudden change had profound implications for Somalia's military capabilities and its overall strategy in the region.

The civil war that erupted in Somalia in 1991 led to the complete breakdown of the central government, resulting in a power vacuum that has never been successfully filled. The absence of a stable government has perpetuated lawlessness and violence across the country.

The civil war has resulted in a severe humanitarian crisis, with millions of people displaced both internally and internationally. Food insecurity and lack of basic services have led to widespread suffering, with ongoing appeals for international aid to address the urgent needs of the population.

Title: Vietnamese authorities block the Mekong to bar entry for hundreds of ethnic Vietnamese evicted from Phnom Penh floating homes
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4
After authorities in Phnom Penh ordered in early June the removal of floating homes from waterways in the metropolitan area, resident Minh Yang Kai took his chances on the flow of the Mekong River.
Yang Kai, 69, was born in Vietnam’s Dong Thap province but has lived in Cambodia for about 25 years, most recently in a house on the river in the capital’s Chbar Ampov district. Rather than demolish his home by the June 12 deadline for the city’s floating house eviction, he decided to float downstream and back to the country of his birth.
“It took about four or five days’ time,” Yang Kai told CamboJA of the journey to the border. His wife slept behind him in a hammock on the couple’s floating home, which is now tied up on the Cambodian side of the border near the Ka’am Samnor international checkpoint.
But the journey back into Vietnam is less certain than simply floating over the aquatic boundary. Now, Yang Kai and hundreds of other mostly ethnic Vietnamese residents of the floating homes have been stopped at the border, held back by Vietnamese officials and an apparent blockade of the Mekong made up of sand barges and other large boats. One witness told CamboJA the area is also patrolled by faster, smaller watercraft prohibiting any crossings. With that kind of enforcement, nobody is quite sure when, or if, these marooned families will be allowed to enter Vietnam, especially as authorities point to the ongoing COVID-19 outbreak in that country as a rationale to forbid entry to the floating households.
“The authorities of Vietnam and Cambodia used ships and ferries to block the water border. They do not let us enter,” Yang Kai said.
_The floating homes of mostly ethnic Vietnamese residents evicted from Phnom Penh were blocked in the Mekong at Kandal province’s Leouk Dek district on the Cambodia-Vietnam border, June 28, 2021. CamboJA/ Pring Samrang_
For now, the families at the border are waiting for a more long-term solution in Ka’am Samnor commune, located in the Loeuk Dek district of Kandal province.

Chap Chanvithyea, the district governor, said on Tuesday that approximately 83 floating houses with as many as 436 people had recently arrived in Ka’am Samnor, on the western banks of the Mekong. This aquatic community brought with it about 119 structures for fish farming, which is a key source of income for the river residents.
Even more families are living on the river’s eastern bank, in Prey Veng province. Seng Thea, governor of Peam Chor district said about 70 families making up a total of roughly 170 people have landed in his area with 32 fish farming structures.
Thea said district authorities had inspected the river blockade but that the matter was ultimately for higher-level officials to handle.
“They arrived at Vietnam’s border but Vietnam dismissed them,” he said. “They used ships to pull their floating house about 200 meters from the border line.”
He said representatives from the ethnic Vietnamese civil society in Cambodia had brought supplies several days ago to floating house residents as they waited in hopes of crossing the demarcation. Some of the people now on the banks do not have Cambodian identification cards, Thea said, but others have permanent residency and have lived in the country since 1979.
Though many of the ethnic Vietnamese people who live on Cambodia’s waterways are stateless, that isn’t true for all. Chanvithyea said those who have arrived in Loeuk Dek district also have Cambodian residency documents. The district governor said local officials are working with members of the floating households to ensure they don’t stay too long.
“We prepared the order for them and we do not allow them to live with anarchy and they also made the contract with our authorities,” Chanvithyea said. “They are not allowed to live here permanently but we will allow them to stay temporarily until their fish are big enough for them to sell. Then they will remove their floating houses by themselves.”
Kandal provincial governor Kong Sophorn also emphasized that the floating houses would only be a short-term fixture. He said authorities would resolve the situation without discrimination or violence but with respect for human rights.
“We implement this case based on the law,” Sophorn said, pointing out the permanent residency status of some of the residents to add that these people are legally allowed to live in Cambodia.

_The floating homes of mostly ethnic Vietnamese residents evicted from Phnom Penh were blocked in the Mekong at Kandal province’s Leouk Dek district on the Cambodia-Vietnam border, June 28, 2021. CamboJA/ Pring Samrang_
Still, for those who are now waiting along the banks for either passage into Vietnam or for their farmed fish to mature, this transitional period is turning out to be a long one.
Yang Thi Neu, 25, is now staying in a floating home in Ka’am Samnor commune. She told CamboJA at the riverbank that originally she’d come from Phnom Penh’s Prek Pnov district, where she was born, after the eviction order. But as with Yang Kai, she continued, once her family reached the border, Vietnamese authorities turned them away, citing the COVID-19 situation.
“Now, we are facing difficulty because we cannot do any business or fishing. We do not have anyone to buy the fish that we are farming,” Thi Neu said. “We don’t have income now, so we just sleep and eat.”
Even once the fish are ready for sale, there’s no guarantee they’ll raise enough money to keep community members financially afloat.
Yang Kai told CamboJA he’d borrowed a total of $12,000 from four lenders in the capital’s Chbar Ampov district to fund his fish farm. Now, he’s not sure who will buy the fish when they’re finally big enough.
“Two debtors followed me here and they demanded their money back — but I do not have money to pay them because I have not sold my fish yet,” he said.
The evictions in Phnom Penh called to attention once again the makeshift conditions of those living on the water.
At the time the notice to clear out was made public, many residents told CamboJA that they did not want to live on the water, citing safety concerns on their floating structures. But with no clear options to resettle on land, especially for those residents who are officially stateless, the rivers of Cambodia have had to make do for a home.

Phnom Penh deputy Governor Keut Chhe told CamboJA that the full number of people living on the waterways has not been fully recorded in the past. However, he said authorities in 2019 had counted the families living on the water in Prek Pnov district and later found that the floating houses and other unpermitted structures in the river had increased.
“If you build a house on land, you will have to apply for a permit and be written down as a statistic,” he said, explaining the localized nature of counting floating houses. “[River residents] just do it and we cannot collect the statistics, so we follow the real situation.”
On June 12, Chhe said the people living in floating houses had generally cooperated with the municipality’s decision to remove what it described as illegal residences on the river. He told CamboJA that households managing fish farms would be allowed to stay on the edge of Phnom Penh between the city’s Prek Pnov district and Kandal province until their fish were old enough to be sold. However, he said then, the people who just have floating houses but do not raise fish would need to find their own housing elsewhere.
_Phnom Penh authorities ordered floating home residents to move down the Tonle Sap to temporarily relocate in Prek Phnov district on the border of Kandal province. Residents may now stay there for six months to finish raising their crop of farmed fish, June 25, 2021. CamboJA/ Pring Samrang_
Nguveng Yang Hong, 46, is one of those people now waiting in Prek Pnov near the provincial border.
Born in Kampong Chhnang province in 1975, Yang Hong and his family left Cambodia for Vietnam before returning to the kingdom in 1982. He had lived in Prek Pnov for more than 10 years before the eviction order came through.
He said the Vietnamese embassy in Phnom Penh and the Association of Khmer-Vietnamese in the Kingdom had helped arrange with authorities to allow residents to stay until their fish matured. After that, Yang Hong isn’t sure where he’ll go.
“After six months, it depends on the authorities and where they order us to live,” he said. “If they do not allow us to live in floating houses, we will find any rental houses to live in.”

Neither Sim Chy, president of the Khmer-Vietnamese Association, nor the Vietnamese embassy provided comment to CamboJA. Keo Vanthan, spokesman of the Cambodian General Department of Immigration, also could not be reached for comment.
Ny Sokha, head of the monitoring section at human rights group Adhoc, said immigration concerns are found across the world, but said countries need to receive their people if and when they are deported from other places. He pointed to deportations of Cambodian nationals from the US as an example.
“So for Vietnamese immigrants, if they come to live in Cambodia legally, Cambodia must respond to solve the problem of removing their homes from the river and allowing them to live anywhere appropriate,” Sokha said. “But if they came to live illegally, it means that they are illegal immigrants, so we must deport them to their country.”
Still, the matter is less clear with individuals of Vietnamese descent who are born and raised in Cambodia and possibly without documentation of any kind.
Pech Pisey, executive director of the Cambodia office of rights monitor Transparency International, said enforcement of immigration law is important but must be done with respect to human rights. He said Cambodia should push back against Vietnam’s use of COVID-19 as a reason to reject its nationals and said the countries should work together to find a solution.
“Vietnam is concerned about COVID but receiving their citizens is not a worry,” Pisey said. “We must push Vietnam to cooperate with sending nationals back to their country as per the law.” **_(Additional reporting by Chea Sokny)_**

# Hundreds evicted from Cambodian floating villages
Most are ethnic Vietnamese with nowhere to go as borders remain closed amid the pandemic
A floating village at Kampong Phuluk on the Tonle Sap. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons/CC BY 2.0)
By UCA News reporter, Phnom Penh
Published: June 16, 2021 06:00 AM GMT
Updated: June 16, 2021 06:19 AM GMT
Share
Add as a preferred source on Google
Authorities in Cambodian capital Phnom Penh have been sharply criticized for evicting hundreds of people and dismantling their house boats on the Mekong River, where families have carved out a lifestyle around fishing for generations.
Embittered residents of the floating communities say they have nowhere to go, particularly amid the pandemic, which has limited travel and resulted in the closure of the border with Vietnam.
Eviction notices, with little warning, were issued by the Phnom Penh Municipality following complaints the communities were little more than "floating slums" littered with plastic bags, raw sewage and other refuse along the Tonle Sap, a tributary of the Mekong.
“There are 316 homes that we have to evict today. This really affects the beauty of the city, the environment. You sit on a boat, it smells very bad,” Si Vutha, head of Prek Pnov district's land management office, told Reuters news agency on June 11.
The evictions are part of a clean-up campaign in the capital as Cambodia takes the rotating chair of the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) next year and hosts the Southeast Asian Games in 2023 with national elections scheduled shortly afterwards.
With nowhere to go and unable to cross the border, Lyo Van Tran, a US-based Vietnamese advocate, urged a delay, saying the exodus could result in a backlog along the closed border that could pose a Covid-19 health risk.
> _**Cambodian government spokesperson Phay Siphan said the evictions followed orders by the National Assembly**_
Critics also argue the evictions reflect a traditional animosity between Khmers and Vietnamese which has resulted in ethnic Vietnamese leaving Cambodia.
Vu Quang Minh, Vietnam’s ambassador to Phnom Penh, has reportedly visited the communities at least twice.

# Hundreds evicted from Cambodian floating villages
But Cambodian government spokesperson Phay Siphan said the evictions followed orders by the National Assembly and the decision was not motivated by politics or discrimination against anyone.
Le Thị Thu Hang, spokesperson for the Vietnamese Foreign Ministry, said her government was providing support and was working with Cambodian authorities to grant legal papers to the affected families.
She said Vietnamese Foreign Minister Bui Thanh Son had asked his Cambodian counterpart Prak Sokhonnto to address the legal status of ethnic Vietnamese living in Cambodia.
“He also asked that the Cambodian authorities have a reasonable roadmap in the implementation of their socioeconomic policies to ensure the rights and welfare of the Vietnamese community,” she told Vietnam News.

Cambodia has endured severe lockdowns since a sharp spike in the Covid-19 pandemic emerged in February which civil society groups like Human Rights Watch (HRW) say has hit low-income families hard despite government handouts.

texts.0:
After authorities in Phnom Penh ordered in early June the removal of floating homes from waterways in the metropolitan area, resident Minh Yang Kai took his chances on the flow of the Mekong River.
Yang Kai, 69, was born in Vietnam’s Dong Thap province but has lived in Cambodia for about 25 years, most recently in a house on the river in the capital’s Chbar Ampov district. Rather than demolish his home by the June 12 deadline for the city’s floating house eviction, he decided to float downstream and back to the country of his birth.
“It took about four or five days’ time,” Yang Kai told CamboJA of the journey to the border. His wife slept behind him in a hammock on the couple’s floating home, which is now tied up on the Cambodian side of the border near the Ka’am Samnor international checkpoint.
But the journey back into Vietnam is less certain than simply floating over the aquatic boundary. Now, Yang Kai and hundreds of other mostly ethnic Vietnamese residents of the floating homes have been stopped at the border, held back by Vietnamese officials and an apparent blockade of the Mekong made up of sand barges and other large boats. One witness told CamboJA the area is also patrolled by faster, smaller watercraft prohibiting any crossings. With that kind of enforcement, nobody is quite sure when, or if, these marooned families will be allowed to enter Vietnam, especially as authorities point to the ongoing COVID-19 outbreak in that country as a rationale to forbid entry to the floating households.
“The authorities of Vietnam and Cambodia used ships and ferries to block the water border. They do not let us enter,” Yang Kai said.
_The floating homes of mostly ethnic Vietnamese residents evicted from Phnom Penh were blocked in the Mekong at Kandal province’s Leouk Dek district on the Cambodia-Vietnam border, June 28, 2021. CamboJA/ Pring Samrang_
For now, the families at the border are waiting for a more long-term solution in Ka’am Samnor commune, located in the Loeuk Dek district of Kandal province.
texts.1:
Chap Chanvithyea, the district governor, said on Tuesday that approximately 83 floating houses with as many as 436 people had recently arrived in Ka’am Samnor, on the western banks of the Mekong. This aquatic community brought with it about 119 structures for fish farming, which is a key source of income for the river residents.
Even more families are living on the river’s eastern bank, in Prey Veng province. Seng Thea, governor of Peam Chor district said about 70 families making up a total of roughly 170 people have landed in his area with 32 fish farming structures.
Thea said district authorities had inspected the river blockade but that the matter was ultimately for higher-level officials to handle.
“They arrived at Vietnam’s border but Vietnam dismissed them,” he said. “They used ships to pull their floating house about 200 meters from the border line.”
He said representatives from the ethnic Vietnamese civil society in Cambodia had brought supplies several days ago to floating house residents as they waited in hopes of crossing the demarcation. Some of the people now on the banks do not have Cambodian identification cards, Thea said, but others have permanent residency and have lived in the country since 1979.
Though many of the ethnic Vietnamese people who live on Cambodia’s waterways are stateless, that isn’t true for all. Chanvithyea said those who have arrived in Loeuk Dek district also have Cambodian residency documents. The district governor said local officials are working with members of the floating households to ensure they don’t stay too long.
“We prepared the order for them and we do not allow them to live with anarchy and they also made the contract with our authorities,” Chanvithyea said. “They are not allowed to live here permanently but we will allow them to stay temporarily until their fish are big enough for them to sell. Then they will remove their floating houses by themselves.”
Kandal provincial governor Kong Sophorn also emphasized that the floating houses would only be a short-term fixture. He said authorities would resolve the situation without discrimination or violence but with respect for human rights.
“We implement this case based on the law,” Sophorn said, pointing out the permanent residency status of some of the residents to add that these people are legally allowed to live in Cambodia.
texts.2:
_The floating homes of mostly ethnic Vietnamese residents evicted from Phnom Penh were blocked in the Mekong at Kandal province’s Leouk Dek district on the Cambodia-Vietnam border, June 28, 2021. CamboJA/ Pring Samrang_
Still, for those who are now waiting along the banks for either passage into Vietnam or for their farmed fish to mature, this transitional period is turning out to be a long one.
Yang Thi Neu, 25, is now staying in a floating home in Ka’am Samnor commune. She told CamboJA at the riverbank that originally she’d come from Phnom Penh’s Prek Pnov district, where she was born, after the eviction order. But as with Yang Kai, she continued, once her family reached the border, Vietnamese authorities turned them away, citing the COVID-19 situation.
“Now, we are facing difficulty because we cannot do any business or fishing. We do not have anyone to buy the fish that we are farming,” Thi Neu said. “We don’t have income now, so we just sleep and eat.”
Even once the fish are ready for sale, there’s no guarantee they’ll raise enough money to keep community members financially afloat.
Yang Kai told CamboJA he’d borrowed a total of $12,000 from four lenders in the capital’s Chbar Ampov district to fund his fish farm. Now, he’s not sure who will buy the fish when they’re finally big enough.
“Two debtors followed me here and they demanded their money back — but I do not have money to pay them because I have not sold my fish yet,” he said.
The evictions in Phnom Penh called to attention once again the makeshift conditions of those living on the water.
At the time the notice to clear out was made public, many residents told CamboJA that they did not want to live on the water, citing safety concerns on their floating structures. But with no clear options to resettle on land, especially for those residents who are officially stateless, the rivers of Cambodia have had to make do for a home.
texts.3:
Phnom Penh deputy Governor Keut Chhe told CamboJA that the full number of people living on the waterways has not been fully recorded in the past. However, he said authorities in 2019 had counted the families living on the water in Prek Pnov district and later found that the floating houses and other unpermitted structures in the river had increased.
“If you build a house on land, you will have to apply for a permit and be written down as a statistic,” he said, explaining the localized nature of counting floating houses. “[River residents] just do it and we cannot collect the statistics, so we follow the real situation.”
On June 12, Chhe said the people living in floating houses had generally cooperated with the municipality’s decision to remove what it described as illegal residences on the river. He told CamboJA that households managing fish farms would be allowed to stay on the edge of Phnom Penh between the city’s Prek Pnov district and Kandal province until their fish were old enough to be sold. However, he said then, the people who just have floating houses but do not raise fish would need to find their own housing elsewhere.
_Phnom Penh authorities ordered floating home residents to move down the Tonle Sap to temporarily relocate in Prek Phnov district on the border of Kandal province. Residents may now stay there for six months to finish raising their crop of farmed fish, June 25, 2021. CamboJA/ Pring Samrang_
Nguveng Yang Hong, 46, is one of those people now waiting in Prek Pnov near the provincial border.
Born in Kampong Chhnang province in 1975, Yang Hong and his family left Cambodia for Vietnam before returning to the kingdom in 1982. He had lived in Prek Pnov for more than 10 years before the eviction order came through.
He said the Vietnamese embassy in Phnom Penh and the Association of Khmer-Vietnamese in the Kingdom had helped arrange with authorities to allow residents to stay until their fish matured. After that, Yang Hong isn’t sure where he’ll go.
“After six months, it depends on the authorities and where they order us to live,” he said. “If they do not allow us to live in floating houses, we will find any rental houses to live in.”
texts.4:
Neither Sim Chy, president of the Khmer-Vietnamese Association, nor the Vietnamese embassy provided comment to CamboJA. Keo Vanthan, spokesman of the Cambodian General Department of Immigration, also could not be reached for comment.
Ny Sokha, head of the monitoring section at human rights group Adhoc, said immigration concerns are found across the world, but said countries need to receive their people if and when they are deported from other places. He pointed to deportations of Cambodian nationals from the US as an example.
“So for Vietnamese immigrants, if they come to live in Cambodia legally, Cambodia must respond to solve the problem of removing their homes from the river and allowing them to live anywhere appropriate,” Sokha said. “But if they came to live illegally, it means that they are illegal immigrants, so we must deport them to their country.”
Still, the matter is less clear with individuals of Vietnamese descent who are born and raised in Cambodia and possibly without documentation of any kind.
Pech Pisey, executive director of the Cambodia office of rights monitor Transparency International, said enforcement of immigration law is important but must be done with respect to human rights. He said Cambodia should push back against Vietnam’s use of COVID-19 as a reason to reject its nationals and said the countries should work together to find a solution.
“Vietnam is concerned about COVID but receiving their citizens is not a worry,” Pisey said. “We must push Vietnam to cooperate with sending nationals back to their country as per the law.” **_(Additional reporting by Chea Sokny)_**

Title: Vietnamese authorities block the Mekong to bar entry for hundreds of ethnic Vietnamese evicted from Phnom Penh floating homes
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4
After authorities in Phnom Penh ordered in early June the removal of floating homes from waterways in the metropolitan area, resident Minh Yang Kai took his chances on the flow of the Mekong River.
Yang Kai, 69, was born in Vietnam’s Dong Thap province but has lived in Cambodia for about 25 years, most recently in a house on the river in the capital’s Chbar Ampov district. Rather than demolish his home by the June 12 deadline for the city’s floating house eviction, he decided to float downstream and back to the country of his birth.
“It took about four or five days’ time,” Yang Kai told CamboJA of the journey to the border. His wife slept behind him in a hammock on the couple’s floating home, which is now tied up on the Cambodian side of the border near the Ka’am Samnor international checkpoint.
But the journey back into Vietnam is less certain than simply floating over the aquatic boundary. Now, Yang Kai and hundreds of other mostly ethnic Vietnamese residents of the floating homes have been stopped at the border, held back by Vietnamese officials and an apparent blockade of the Mekong made up of sand barges and other large boats. One witness told CamboJA the area is also patrolled by faster, smaller watercraft prohibiting any crossings. With that kind of enforcement, nobody is quite sure when, or if, these marooned families will be allowed to enter Vietnam, especially as authorities point to the ongoing COVID-19 outbreak in that country as a rationale to forbid entry to the floating households.
“The authorities of Vietnam and Cambodia used ships and ferries to block the water border. They do not let us enter,” Yang Kai said.
_The floating homes of mostly ethnic Vietnamese residents evicted from Phnom Penh were blocked in the Mekong at Kandal province’s Leouk Dek district on the Cambodia-Vietnam border, June 28, 2021. CamboJA/ Pring Samrang_
For now, the families at the border are waiting for a more long-term solution in Ka’am Samnor commune, located in the Loeuk Dek district of Kandal province.

Chap Chanvithyea, the district governor, said on Tuesday that approximately 83 floating houses with as many as 436 people had recently arrived in Ka’am Samnor, on the western banks of the Mekong. This aquatic community brought with it about 119 structures for fish farming, which is a key source of income for the river residents.
Even more families are living on the river’s eastern bank, in Prey Veng province. Seng Thea, governor of Peam Chor district said about 70 families making up a total of roughly 170 people have landed in his area with 32 fish farming structures.
Thea said district authorities had inspected the river blockade but that the matter was ultimately for higher-level officials to handle.
“They arrived at Vietnam’s border but Vietnam dismissed them,” he said. “They used ships to pull their floating house about 200 meters from the border line.”
He said representatives from the ethnic Vietnamese civil society in Cambodia had brought supplies several days ago to floating house residents as they waited in hopes of crossing the demarcation. Some of the people now on the banks do not have Cambodian identification cards, Thea said, but others have permanent residency and have lived in the country since 1979.
Though many of the ethnic Vietnamese people who live on Cambodia’s waterways are stateless, that isn’t true for all. Chanvithyea said those who have arrived in Loeuk Dek district also have Cambodian residency documents. The district governor said local officials are working with members of the floating households to ensure they don’t stay too long.
“We prepared the order for them and we do not allow them to live with anarchy and they also made the contract with our authorities,” Chanvithyea said. “They are not allowed to live here permanently but we will allow them to stay temporarily until their fish are big enough for them to sell. Then they will remove their floating houses by themselves.”
Kandal provincial governor Kong Sophorn also emphasized that the floating houses would only be a short-term fixture. He said authorities would resolve the situation without discrimination or violence but with respect for human rights.
“We implement this case based on the law,” Sophorn said, pointing out the permanent residency status of some of the residents to add that these people are legally allowed to live in Cambodia.

_The floating homes of mostly ethnic Vietnamese residents evicted from Phnom Penh were blocked in the Mekong at Kandal province’s Leouk Dek district on the Cambodia-Vietnam border, June 28, 2021. CamboJA/ Pring Samrang_
Still, for those who are now waiting along the banks for either passage into Vietnam or for their farmed fish to mature, this transitional period is turning out to be a long one.
Yang Thi Neu, 25, is now staying in a floating home in Ka’am Samnor commune. She told CamboJA at the riverbank that originally she’d come from Phnom Penh’s Prek Pnov district, where she was born, after the eviction order. But as with Yang Kai, she continued, once her family reached the border, Vietnamese authorities turned them away, citing the COVID-19 situation.
“Now, we are facing difficulty because we cannot do any business or fishing. We do not have anyone to buy the fish that we are farming,” Thi Neu said. “We don’t have income now, so we just sleep and eat.”
Even once the fish are ready for sale, there’s no guarantee they’ll raise enough money to keep community members financially afloat.
Yang Kai told CamboJA he’d borrowed a total of $12,000 from four lenders in the capital’s Chbar Ampov district to fund his fish farm. Now, he’s not sure who will buy the fish when they’re finally big enough.
“Two debtors followed me here and they demanded their money back — but I do not have money to pay them because I have not sold my fish yet,” he said.
The evictions in Phnom Penh called to attention once again the makeshift conditions of those living on the water.
At the time the notice to clear out was made public, many residents told CamboJA that they did not want to live on the water, citing safety concerns on their floating structures. But with no clear options to resettle on land, especially for those residents who are officially stateless, the rivers of Cambodia have had to make do for a home.

Phnom Penh deputy Governor Keut Chhe told CamboJA that the full number of people living on the waterways has not been fully recorded in the past. However, he said authorities in 2019 had counted the families living on the water in Prek Pnov district and later found that the floating houses and other unpermitted structures in the river had increased.
“If you build a house on land, you will have to apply for a permit and be written down as a statistic,” he said, explaining the localized nature of counting floating houses. “[River residents] just do it and we cannot collect the statistics, so we follow the real situation.”
On June 12, Chhe said the people living in floating houses had generally cooperated with the municipality’s decision to remove what it described as illegal residences on the river. He told CamboJA that households managing fish farms would be allowed to stay on the edge of Phnom Penh between the city’s Prek Pnov district and Kandal province until their fish were old enough to be sold. However, he said then, the people who just have floating houses but do not raise fish would need to find their own housing elsewhere.
_Phnom Penh authorities ordered floating home residents to move down the Tonle Sap to temporarily relocate in Prek Phnov district on the border of Kandal province. Residents may now stay there for six months to finish raising their crop of farmed fish, June 25, 2021. CamboJA/ Pring Samrang_
Nguveng Yang Hong, 46, is one of those people now waiting in Prek Pnov near the provincial border.
Born in Kampong Chhnang province in 1975, Yang Hong and his family left Cambodia for Vietnam before returning to the kingdom in 1982. He had lived in Prek Pnov for more than 10 years before the eviction order came through.
He said the Vietnamese embassy in Phnom Penh and the Association of Khmer-Vietnamese in the Kingdom had helped arrange with authorities to allow residents to stay until their fish matured. After that, Yang Hong isn’t sure where he’ll go.
“After six months, it depends on the authorities and where they order us to live,” he said. “If they do not allow us to live in floating houses, we will find any rental houses to live in.”

Neither Sim Chy, president of the Khmer-Vietnamese Association, nor the Vietnamese embassy provided comment to CamboJA. Keo Vanthan, spokesman of the Cambodian General Department of Immigration, also could not be reached for comment.
Ny Sokha, head of the monitoring section at human rights group Adhoc, said immigration concerns are found across the world, but said countries need to receive their people if and when they are deported from other places. He pointed to deportations of Cambodian nationals from the US as an example.
“So for Vietnamese immigrants, if they come to live in Cambodia legally, Cambodia must respond to solve the problem of removing their homes from the river and allowing them to live anywhere appropriate,” Sokha said. “But if they came to live illegally, it means that they are illegal immigrants, so we must deport them to their country.”
Still, the matter is less clear with individuals of Vietnamese descent who are born and raised in Cambodia and possibly without documentation of any kind.
Pech Pisey, executive director of the Cambodia office of rights monitor Transparency International, said enforcement of immigration law is important but must be done with respect to human rights. He said Cambodia should push back against Vietnam’s use of COVID-19 as a reason to reject its nationals and said the countries should work together to find a solution.
“Vietnam is concerned about COVID but receiving their citizens is not a worry,” Pisey said. “We must push Vietnam to cooperate with sending nationals back to their country as per the law.” **_(Additional reporting by Chea Sokny)_**

*The “same people” are the **Portuguese**.*

1. **Ajuran Empire – “declared independence”**  
   • In the 16th century the Ajuran Sultanate of Somalia confronted the expanding Portuguese naval presence on the East African coast.  
   • Through a series of naval battles and diplomatic incidents the Ajuran managed to **expel the Portuguese fleet from its protector‑city (e.g., Mogadishu, Barawa, Zeila)** and thereby declared *independence* – or at least a practical withdrawal – of Portuguese influence from its realms.  

2. **Expulsion from the Mekong‑border (between Thailand & Laos – Khong Island)**  
   • The same Portuguese forces that had been pushed out of the Somali coast later operated on the Mekong River, which forms a natural boundary between **Thailand and Laos** (the location of Khong Island).  
   • After the Siamese monarchy consolidated its control over the upper Mekong, the Portuguese were **expelled from the river to the north of Khong Island** in the late 17th‑early 18th centuries, when Siam/Thais moved to eliminate foreign naval presence on the river.  

So, the Portuguese — expelled from the Ajuran Empire’s coastal holdings — were again expelled from the Mekong‑river boundary that separates Thailand and Laos, the country that hosts Khong Island.
